steps.title: One parcel
steps.short: From 1667 the Williams family farm here. The Williams-Buckler family asserts they were never squatters, but virtual freeholders.
steps.text: Mary (Nancy) Williams’s witness statement puts the start of the Williams family’s occupation in 1667 (Master Timeline; an earlier written source is awaited). The Williams-Buckler family asserts that from then the family are virtual freeholders of the holding, never squatters. The tithe survey of about 1841 lists the Bute estate as owner and John Williams as occupier of the holding. Until 1877 it is drawn here as one parcel. The outline is a reconstruction.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: From sixteen sixty-seven the Williams family farm here. The Williams-Buckler family asserts they were never squatters, but virtual freeholders.

steps.title: The split: Parcel A and Parcel B
steps.short: In 1877 it is split in two: Parcel A and Parcel B.
steps.text: Mary (Nancy) Williams later stated that in 1877 the Bute estate sold the farmhouse, its buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas & Son, the lime-works firm, and kept about 9 acres. The Williams-Buckler family’s case calls these Parcel A (west: wood, house and yard, green) and Parcel B (the fields to the east). The 1877 deed and plan are missing, so the lines on this step are a reconstruction.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In eighteen seventy-seven it is split in two: Parcel A and Parcel B.

steps.title: Two freeholds
steps.short: Until 1928, a lime-works firm holds the freehold of Parcel A, and Bute holds Parcel B.
steps.text: The Williams-Buckler family asserts that from 1877 to 1928 the freehold of Parcel A sits with Daniel Thomas & Son and the freehold of Parcel B with the Bute estate. The Ordnance Survey 25-inch sheet (revised 1898, published 1900) shows the farmyard as field 70 (1·334 acres); the Williams plan in the family papers was traced from this sheet.

img.cap: The Williams plan (left) beside the 1900 OS sheet (right)

steps.say: Until nineteen twenty-eight, a lime-works firm holds the freehold of Parcel A, and Bute holds Parcel B.

steps.title: The last tenancy of Parcel A
steps.short: In 1916 the family sign the last tenancy of Parcel A.
steps.text: In February 1916 John Williams took a yearly agricultural tenancy; the 1987 judgment describes it as a tenancy of the "whole farm". The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was the last tenancy of Parcel A, and that the Williams family had been virtual freeholders since 1667. The paper freeholds stay with Thomas (Parcel A) and Bute (Parcel B). The 1916 tenancy itself (EV-0014) is not held.
steps.say: In nineteen sixteen the family sign the last tenancy of Parcel A.

steps.title: Parcel A to the Williams family
steps.short: In 1928 the last rent for Parcel A is paid. From then, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, Parcel A is the Williams family’s own.
steps.text: Mary (Nancy) Williams’s statement: the quarry machinery left in 1928 and her father paid the last rent, about £4 a year, to Alfred Thomas. "After this my father regarded the farm as his own." The Williams-Buckler family asserts that from 1928 the Williams family are the freeholders of Parcel A. The receipt is not held.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen twenty-eight the last rent for Parcel A is paid. From then, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, Parcel A is the Williams family’s own.

steps.title: Western Ground Rents
steps.short: In 1938 Western Ground Rents buy Parcel B, and the interest in the 1916 agreement.
steps.text: The sale was announced on 17 May 1938 and completed in December 1938; later deeds recite "a Conveyance on sale dated 25th December 1938" as the root of title. The Williams-Buckler family asserts that what Western Ground Rents bought was the Bute freehold of Parcel B and the Bute interest under the 1916 agreement. The 1938 deed and its plan are not held, so exactly which land it conveyed is the open question.
steps.say: In nineteen thirty-eight Western Ground Rents buy Parcel B, and the interest in the nineteen sixteen agreement.

steps.title: Parcel B only
steps.short: In 1939 a new agreement covers Parcel B only. Parcel A stands apart.
steps.text: In May 1939 Western Ground Rents gave John Williams a new agreement (Glamorgan Archives DBDT123/7), a monthly let "as meadow or pasture land". Its plan colours only the fields east of the house: Parcel B. The house, yard, wood and green are not coloured. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this shows Parcel A had severed from what was conveyed in 1938.

img.cap: DBDT123/7, 1939 plan: the coloured fields east of the house

steps.say: In nineteen thirty-nine a new agreement covers Parcel B only. Parcel A stands apart.

steps.title: The twelve-year rule
steps.short: In 1940 a new Limitation Act takes effect. After twelve rent-free years, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, Parcel A is the family’s.
steps.text: The Limitation Act 1939 came into force on 1 July 1940 (s.34(2)). Under s.4(3) no action to recover land may be brought more than twelve years after the right to bring it arose, and under s.16 the paper owner’s title then ends. (A twelve-year period for land goes back to the Real Property Limitation Act 1874.) By then, on Mary (Nancy) Williams’s statement that the last rent was paid in 1928, the family had held Parcel A rent-free for twelve years. The Williams-Buckler family treats this rule as the key to what followed.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen forty a new Limitation Act takes effect. After twelve rent-free years, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, Parcel A is the family’s.

steps.title: Leckwith Woods to Cardiff
steps.short: In 1942 Western Ground Rents complete a gift of about 109 acres of Leckwith Woods to Cardiff council.
steps.text: Western Ground Rents gave about 109 acres of Leckwith Woods to Cardiff council: offered and accepted in 1940, completed in April 1942 (Master Timeline; EV-0220, a secondary source; the deed and its plan are not held).
steps.say: In nineteen forty-two Western Ground Rents complete a gift of about a hundred and nine acres of Leckwith Woods to Cardiff council.

steps.title: The woodland splits off
steps.short: In 1949, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, an attempt begins to make Mary’s hold on Parcel A look permissive, starting with the woodland.
steps.text: The Williams-Buckler family asserts that in 1949 Mary (Nancy) Williams rejected an attempt by Western Ground Rents to bring her under a tenancy, and that attempt concerned the woodland, the top third of Parcel A. From here the woodland begins to be treated as a parcel of its own: a synthetic parcel carved from A (shown dashed until it is registered). No document of the 1949 offer is held yet.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen forty-nine, the Williams-Buckler family asserts, an attempt begins to make Mary’s hold on Parcel A look permissive, starting with the woodland.

steps.title: Her paper title
steps.short: Between 1950 and 1952 the family papers are taken. The Williams-Buckler family asserts they included Mary’s title to Parcel A.
steps.text: The family papers, including the farm agreement, were taken from the blanket box in 1950–52. The Williams-Buckler family asserts that Mary (Nancy) Williams’s paper title to Parcel A was among them. Her own statement records how; no person is named here. The family also asserts a link between this loss and the later attempts to take her home and land.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: Between nineteen fifty and nineteen fifty-two the family papers are taken. The Williams-Buckler family asserts they included Mary’s title to Parcel A.

steps.title: 4 July 1955
steps.short: On 4 July 1955 a possession order is enforced on every part of the farm except the farmhouse and garden. Parcel A’s woodland and green are taken.
steps.text: After a notice to quit expired on 2 February 1955, Western Ground Rents obtained a High Court possession order (Order 14) against Frederick Buckler “in respect of the whole of the farm”. The Court of Appeal’s 1987 judgment records: “On July 4 1955 that possession order was enforced, and possession was taken in respect of all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden.” Parcel A’s parts outside the farmhouse and garden are its woodland (top third) and its green (lower third), so both were taken that day (Three Parts of Parcel A; 1955 Parcel-A Loss Dossier). In 1958 Mary (Nancy) Williams named who had taken the land (see 1958). The Williams-Buckler family asserts the order concerned Parcel B and that its “whole farm” wording was used to take the woodland and the green. The order’s plan and the execution return are not held.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: On the fourth of July, nineteen fifty-five a possession order is enforced on every part of the farm except the farmhouse and garden. Parcel A’s woodland and green are taken.

steps.title: The attempt on the farmhouse
steps.short: The order also covers the farmhouse, but it is not enforced there. Mary, just home from hospital after losing her leg, objects very strongly to leaving.
steps.text: The Court of Appeal’s 1987 judgment records that the order “was not enforced in respect of the farmhouse and garden” because Mary “had recently come out of hospital after having had a leg amputated and was objecting very strongly to leaving the farmhouse”. The Williams-Buckler family asserts she could not defend the woodland or the green when they were taken.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: The order also covers the farmhouse, but it is not enforced there. Mary, just home from hospital after losing her leg, objects very strongly to leaving.

steps.title: She objects in public
steps.short: In November 1958 Mary tells Glamorgan County Council’s planning committee that her family’s land has been wrongfully appropriated, naming Glamorgan County Council, Penarth Urban Council, Cardiff Rural Council and Western Ground Rents.
steps.text: The Western Mail of 20 November 1958 (p.7) reports Mrs M. D. Buckler, Mary (Nancy) Williams, at Glamorgan County Council’s planning committee on 19 November 1958. Land farmed by her family since 1667 had been “wrongfully appropriated”; sites had been let “over her head” by Western Ground Rents, one of them used by Penarth Urban Council as a rubbish tip; and “The Glamorgan County Council, Penarth Urban and Cardiff Rural Councils and Western Ground Rents have walked in and taken […]”. She objected publicly in 1958, before the 1961 deed recorded against the woodland and before the green was registered in 1970, so the woodland and the green were not held uncontested from 1955. The newspaper text is read from British Newspaper Archive OCR; the page image is not yet seen.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In November nineteen fifty-eight Mary tells Glamorgan County Council’s planning committee that her family’s land has been wrongfully appropriated, naming Glamorgan County Council, Penarth Urban Council, Cardiff Rural Council and Western Ground Rents.

steps.title: She refuses a tenancy
steps.short: By 1959 Western Ground Rents offer Mary a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden, in Parcel A. She refuses, asserting ownership through her grandfather.
steps.text: The Court of Appeal’s 1987 judgment records that by 1959 Mary believed “she had a title to the ownership of Great House Farm through her own grandfather”, and: “She was offered a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden by Western Ground Rents but refused to accept it.” The offer itself (EV-0039) is not held; the Legal Wiki records the 1959 and 1965 offers as concerning the remaining house and garden. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was the second attempt to make her occupation of Parcel A look permissive.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: By nineteen fifty-nine Western Ground Rents offer Mary a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden, in Parcel A. She refuses, asserting ownership through her grandfather.

steps.title: The 1961 deed
steps.short: In March 1961 a deed is made between Western Ground Rents, the South Western Brick and Tile Company and Cardiff City Corporation. The title of Parcel A’s woodland is later recorded as subject to rights under it.
steps.text: HM Land Registry’s register for the woodland, title WA735527, records: “The land tinted pink on the filed plan is subject to the rights contained in a Deed dated 29 March 1961 made between (1) Western Ground Rents Limited (2) The South Western Brick & Tile Company Limited and (3) Cardiff City Corporation.” A copy of the deed is filed under title WA231076; the deed and its plan have not yet been inspected (EV-0040). The same register records a conveyance of 23 May 1975 from The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited to B.P. Properties Limited, and names Forest of Cardiff (company 2591796) as proprietor from 25 November 1994.
steps.say: In March nineteen sixty-one a deed is made between Western Ground Rents, the South Western Brick and Tile Company and Cardiff City Corporation. The title of Parcel A’s woodland is later recorded as subject to rights under it.

steps.title: The 1962 order
steps.short: In December 1962 a court order is made for the farmhouse and garden, in Parcel A, but it is not enforced.
steps.text: On 11 December 1962 Cardiff County Court ordered possession of the farmhouse and garden. The Court of Appeal records that “nothing was done before 1974 to enforce the 1962 possession order”. The Williams-Buckler family asserts the order is unenforced and arguably unenforceable, and rests on the ambiguity of the 1955 order, which was for Parcel B.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In December nineteen sixty-two a court order is made for the farmhouse and garden, in Parcel A, but it is not enforced.

steps.title: Refused again
steps.short: In 1965 she refuses a third attempt to make her a tenant.
steps.text: The Court of Appeal records that in March 1965 Western Ground Rents’ agents offered Mrs Buckler a weekly tenancy. It was not signed and no rent was paid. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was the third attempt to make her occupation look permissive.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen sixty-five she refuses a third attempt to make her a tenant.

steps.title: Only Parcel B to BP
steps.short: In 1969 only Parcel B, and the unenforced 1962 order, pass to BP Pension Trust.
steps.text: On 31 December 1969 Western Ground Rents conveyed to BP Pension Trust. The Williams-Buckler family asserts that what passed was Parcel B, plus the benefit of the unenforced 1962 order on Parcel A, not the farm as a whole. Parcel A stayed with the Williams family; the woodland had already been carved out. The 1969 conveyance and its plan are not held.

AM.note: BP Pension Trust now holds the benefit of the unenforced 1962 order.

steps.say: In nineteen sixty-nine only Parcel B, and the unenforced nineteen sixty-two order, pass to BP Pension Trust.

steps.title: The green registered
steps.short: In 1970 the green, the lower third of Parcel A, is registered as village green VG41. Mary had objected in public in 1958.
steps.text: On 16 June 1970 land by Leckwith Road was registered as village green VG41 (EV-0044). Registrations were publicised by public notice only (EV-0263). The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was the lower third of Parcel A, taken on 4 July 1955, and that Mary’s public objection of November 1958 and her 1959 and 1965 refusals were not put before the registration. The VG41 file and its boundary are not held: the green is drawn here as the lower third of Parcel A, over the ground the 1985 certified register map points to. Llandough Community Council was formed in 1982; before that the village was administered as part of Penarth (Llandough parish was added to the parish of Penarth on 30 September 1902).

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen seventy the green, the lower third of Parcel A, is registered as village green V G forty-one. Mary had objected in public in nineteen fifty-eight.

steps.title: Open day
steps.short: In 1974 Mary opens the farmhouse to the public and, in court, pleads ownership and the Limitation Act 1939.
steps.text: On 15 April 1974 Mary opened the farmhouse to the public, and about 1,000 people signed a petition. In BP Pension Trust’s possession action, adjourned part heard on 3 July 1974, she pleaded ownership (Legal Wiki, Mary page: “1974 — 3 July: pleads ownership and the Limitation Act 1939”), and the Court of Appeal records that her defence pleaded that BP Pension Trust’s action “was barred by adverse possession under the Limitation Act 1939”. That action was never finally heard. On 31 October the warrant was withdrawn and licence letters were sent the same day.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen seventy-four Mary opens the farmhouse to the public and, in court, pleads ownership and the Limitation Act nineteen thirty-nine.

steps.title: To BP Properties
steps.short: In 1975 BP Pension Trust passes its interest to BP Properties.
steps.text: On 23 May 1975 BP Pension Trust conveyed to BP Properties. This conveyance later supported the registration of the house parcel.
steps.say: In nineteen seventy-five BP Pension Trust passes its interest to BP Properties.

steps.title: The tree
steps.short: No earlier than autumn 1980, the tree John Williams planted on Parcel A to prove ownership is removed. Its planting is photographed in the People’s Collection Wales.
steps.text: People’s Collection Wales, the national heritage collection, holds “A black and white photograph of tree planting by John Williams (Grandfather) to prove land ownership at Great House Farm, Llandough” (owner Mary Godfrey; uploaded by Vale of Glamorgan Libraries, 20 August 2018). The tree was removed in an autumn no earlier than 1980: a JCB 3CX badge is legible in the family’s photographs of the removal, and that model was first built in 1980. The exact year is still being established. The Vale of Glamorgan Council is checking whether it holds any record of the removal.

img.cap: John Williams’s tree planting at Great House Farm. Photo: Mary Godfrey / People’s Collection Wales.

steps.say: No earlier than autumn nineteen eighty, the tree John Williams planted on Parcel A to prove ownership is removed. Its planting is photographed in the People’s Collection Wales.

steps.title: First registration: WA231076
steps.short: In 1982 BP Properties applies for its first title: Parcel B, on the Williams-Buckler family’s reconstruction.
steps.text: On 30 November 1982 BP Properties applied for first registration of title WA231076. On the Williams-Buckler family’s reconstruction this is the fields strand: Parcel B.
steps.say: In nineteen eighty-two BP Properties applies for its first title: Parcel B, on the Williams-Buckler family’s reconstruction.

steps.title: First registration: WA240304
steps.short: In 1983 it applies to register the farmhouse too. Mary dies there, never having signed a tenancy.
steps.text: On 23 February 1983 an application followed for title WA240304: the farmhouse and garden, BP's third of Parcel A. Mary died at the farmhouse on 26 March 1983, and William inherited.

img.cap: Mary (Nancy) Williams, formerly Buckler, at Tŷ Mawr. Family photograph.

steps.say: In nineteen eighty-three it applies to register the farmhouse too. Mary dies there, never having signed a tenancy.

steps.title: High Court
steps.short: In 1986 the High Court hears BP Properties v Buckler.
steps.text: On 24 July 1986 the High Court gave judgment in BP Properties v Buckler.
steps.say: In nineteen eighty-six the High Court hears BP Properties versus Buckler.

steps.title: The merger
steps.short: In 1987, during the appeal, an application is made to merge the farmhouse title with Parcel B’s.
steps.text: On 2 February 1987, while the appeal was pending, an application was made to amalgamate the two titles. The house parcel joined the fields. BP's third of Parcel A and Parcel B became one registered title.
steps.say: In nineteen eighty-seven, during the appeal, an application is made to merge the farmhouse title with Parcel B’s.

steps.title: Court of Appeal
steps.short: In July 1987 the Court of Appeal gives judgment in BP Properties v Buckler.
steps.text: On 31 July 1987 the Court of Appeal gave judgment in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2. The appeal was confined to the farmhouse and garden.
steps.say: In July nineteen eighty-seven the Court of Appeal gives judgment in BP Properties versus Buckler.

steps.title: Taken and demolished
steps.short: In 1988 the farmhouse is taken and demolished. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was not the eviction of squatters from Parcel A.
steps.text: In April 1988 the bailiffs were held off. Possession was taken on 30 November, and by 6 December the outbuildings and the farmhouse were demolished. Family recollection, 1988: a courtyard, with the barn to the west, sheds to the north and stables to the south. The wood lay to the north and the green to the south. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was not the eviction of squatters from Parcel A.
steps.say: In nineteen eighty-eight the farmhouse is taken and demolished. The Williams-Buckler family asserts this was not the eviction of squatters from Parcel A.

steps.title: Afterwards
steps.short: Today houses stand on the yard of Parcel A. The woodland is registered to the Forest of Cardiff charity, and the green is village green VG41.
steps.text: On 13 March 1990 outline permission was granted for housing on about 3·4 acres. In 1992 reserved matters were approved for 20 houses. The woodland’s title, WA735527, names Forest of Cardiff as registered proprietor from 25 November 1994. The green remains registered village green VG41. This is the land as it looks today.
steps.say: Today houses stand on the yard of Parcel A. The woodland is registered to the Forest of Cardiff charity, and the green is village green V G forty-one.

markers.text: Unidentified (pond, well, horse-gin or older structure). Drawn on the OS sheets of 1878–79 and 1900.

markers.text: The farmhouse, east side of the yard. Demolished December 1988.

markers.label: Barn (west)
markers.text: Family recollection, 1988: the barn on the west side of the courtyard.

markers.label: Sheds (north)
